passage: In the tuition room above the medical shop in Ottapalam, Trisha sat with a school notebook after the last batch left. A parent had come in at six, upset: her son's English marks hadn't improved in two months. Trisha's first thought was to shut the evening batch altogether. Instead she drew a line down the page. On the left she wrote three things: the Class 7 group's maths average had gone up, two students now read aloud without being asked, and the attendance register was full for the first time. On the right: 'Rehan's English, no improvement. My fault? Partly. I haven't tested his grammar separately.' Deepika, her cousin who helped with the fees, peeped over. 'You're not closing?' 'No,' Trisha said. 'I'm giving Rehan a separate grammar test on Monday.'

qa.q: Where was Trisha's tuition room?
qa.a: Trisha's tuition room was above the medical shop in Ottapalam.

qa.q: Why was Trisha's first thought to shut the evening batch?
qa.a: The parent's complaint stung so much that it seemed to outweigh everything else, making the whole tuition centre feel like a failure for a moment.

qa.q: How did Trisha's two-column page lead to a better decision?
qa.a: Listing three real successes beside the one problem kept the complaint in proportion, and looking honestly at the problem showed a specific fix: a separate grammar test for Rehan.

qa.q: How might the parent feel when told about the grammar test?
qa.a: The parent may feel heard and reassured that the complaint was taken seriously and turned into action.

grounding: Shows an adult tutor who, after a parent's complaint, writes three things going well beside the one that isn't, then acts on the criticism without shutting the class.

passage: On Sunday night in her small flat in Lisbon, Clara read the review of her pastry stall again: one star, 'overpriced and cold'. Her thumb hovered over the button to delete the stall's page. Then she remembered what Rosa had said at the market: before you decide anything, write down three good things first. She took the back of an electricity bill. One: sold out of custard tarts by noon for the third week running. Two: the café on Rua Augusta had asked about a weekly order. Three: an old man came back just to say the orange cake tasted like his mother's. Then a fourth line: 'Tarts sit too long in the afternoon. The review is partly right.' She didn't delete the page. She texted Rosa: 'Buying a warming box. Also, the café wants tarts.'

qa.q: What did the one-star review say?
qa.a: The review said 'overpriced and cold'.

qa.q: Why was Clara about to delete her stall's page?
qa.a: The one-star review hurt, and in that moment it seemed to speak for the whole business, making weeks of success feel like failure.

qa.q: How did the list on the electricity bill help Clara decide?
qa.a: Writing three wins beside the one problem kept the review in proportion, and admitting 'partly right' pointed to a clear fix: a warming box for the afternoon tarts.

qa.q: What might Rosa feel reading Clara's message?
qa.a: Rosa would likely feel glad and relieved that the advice worked, and happy to hear about the café order.

grounding: Shows an adult who, after a harsh review, lists three things that went well beside the fair criticism, then acts on it instead of quitting.

passage:
At the community centre in Guwahati, Kalyani ran the evening computer class for women who had never used email. On Thursday, one learner, Mrs Baruah, complained to the coordinator, Arnab, that Kalyani moved too fast and she felt left behind.

Kalyani's first thought was to hand over the class to someone else.

Instead, after the last learner left, she sat in the empty room with a notebook and drew a line down the middle. On the left, what had worked: eleven of twelve learners sent their first email this month. Two asked for an extra class. Mrs Deka printed a photo of her grandson by herself and cried a little.

On the right, the one thing that didn't: Mrs Baruah felt rushed.

She looked at both sides. The criticism was real. It just wasn't everything.

Next week, she decided, she'd keep the class and add ten minutes at the end for anyone who wanted to go slower. She'd ask Mrs Baruah to stay.

qa.q: How many learners sent their first email this month?
qa.a: Eleven of twelve learners.

qa.q: What was Kalyani probably feeling when her first thought was to hand the class over?
qa.a: She likely felt hurt and ashamed after the complaint, as if one learner's frustration proved she was failing. Quitting seemed like a way to escape that feeling.

qa.q: Why did listing three good things before deciding help, without ignoring the complaint?
qa.a: It gave Kalyani the full picture, so she could see the class was working and still take Mrs Baruah's point seriously. That led to a practical fix, a slower extra ten minutes, rather than quitting.

qa.q: How might Mrs Baruah feel when Kalyani asks her to stay for the slower time?
qa.a: Mrs Baruah would probably feel heard and relieved that her complaint led to real help. She may also feel less alone in finding it hard.

grounding: A young instructor lists three things that went well next to one complaint before deciding what to do, taking the criticism seriously without letting it dominate.

Subject: After my talk

Dear Abhinav sir,

Thank you for pushing me to present at the regional water conference. I wanted to tell you how it went, honestly.

In the question round, a senior engineer said my cost figures looked "naive" and that I hadn't accounted for maintenance. My face went hot. For the first hour after, all I could think was: never presenting again.

Then I did what you taught me and wrote it down properly before deciding anything.

Went well: 1. The room was full, and people stayed after to ask about the village pilot. 2. Two NGOs asked for my slides. 3. I finished on time, which I never used to.

Didn't go well: my cost figures missed maintenance, and he was right.

So my decision is not "never again". It's: rework the cost section with maintenance included, and send it to the engineer to check.

Would you look at the draft next week?

Yusuf

qa.q: How many NGOs asked for Yusuf's slides?
qa.a: Two NGOs asked for the slides.

qa.q: What was Yusuf feeling in the first hour after the question round?
qa.a: Embarrassed and shaken, with a hot face, enough to think of never presenting again. The criticism briefly filled Yusuf's whole view of the talk.

qa.q: What did balancing the ledger help Yusuf decide, and why is it a good decision?
qa.a: Yusuf decided to keep presenting and rework the cost section to include maintenance. It accepts the fair criticism while keeping what went well, instead of quitting.

qa.q: How might the senior engineer react if Yusuf sends the reworked cost section?
qa.a: The engineer might be pleasantly surprised and respect Yusuf for taking the point seriously. It could even turn a harsh moment into a useful connection.

grounding: A young engineer lists three things that went well next to one sharp criticism before deciding what to do, keeping the criticism without letting it rule.

passage: Farida, you asked how I survived my first week running the kitchen. I'll tell you about Thursday. We had forty covers, my biggest night yet, and one table sent back the fish, overcooked. I could feel the whole night collapsing into that one plate. I'm Harsha, I've cooked since I was fifteen, and I still wanted to hide in the cold room. Instead I grabbed an order slip and made two columns. Left side: the dal sold out; the new cook plated fast without mistakes; two tables asked to meet the chef. Right side: fish overcooked, table six. I looked at both. Then I decided: one person would own the fish station on busy nights, with a timer. That was it. The fish was real. So were the other three. You need both columns to know what to fix.

qa.q: How many covers did the kitchen have on Thursday?
qa.a: The kitchen had forty covers.

qa.q: What was Harsha feeling when the fish came back?
qa.a: Harsha felt a rush of embarrassment and dread, as if the whole night was collapsing into that one plate.

qa.q: What did Harsha decide after looking at both columns?
qa.a: That one person would own the fish station on busy nights, with a timer, which fixed the real problem without writing off a good night.

qa.q: How might the new cook see the night if only the fish had been counted?
qa.a: The new cook's fast, clean plating would have gone unnoticed, and the kitchen might have felt like it had failed.

grounding: An adult lists three things that went well beside the one that did not before deciding on a fix, without denying the criticism.

passage: I share a desk with Gopika at the architecture firm, so I saw most of it. On Monday her first presentation to a client came back with a sharp email: the facade was 'too plain for the brief'. She read it, went very still, and then did something I didn't expect. She laid a sheet of tracing paper over her sketchbook and wrote, in her small neat hand: the floor plan they praised; the costs came in under estimate; the client's son loved the courtyard. Then, on the other side: facade too plain. She looked at the two lists for a while. I can't say what she was feeling; her face gave very little away. But after ten minutes she said, 'Harish, can you look at three facade options with me after lunch?' She didn't argue with the email, and she didn't cross out the good lines either.

qa.q: What did the client's email say about the facade?
qa.a: It said the facade was 'too plain for the brief'.

qa.q: What does Gopika's stillness and then her list suggest about how she handled the criticism?
qa.a: It suggests she felt stung but steady, choosing to weigh the criticism next to three real successes before deciding what to do.

qa.q: Why was listing the good points before acting a wise choice?
qa.a: It kept the criticism in proportion without denying it, so her next step was a focused fix, three facade options, rather than panic or defensiveness.

qa.q: How does Harish see Gopika's response?
qa.a: Harish is surprised and impressed that she neither argued with the email nor let it wipe out the good lines.

grounding: A colleague describes an architect listing three things that went well beside one sharp criticism before choosing a fix.

Monday. A parent's note arrived in Reena's pigeonhole: her Class 4 maths homework was 'too much for small children'. Reena read it three times in the staffroom and felt her face go hot. She'd only been teaching six weeks.
Tuesday. Before deciding anything, she opened her planner and wrote on one side: the class finished the fractions unit on time; three shy children now put up their hands; the head praised her board work. Omkar, your first week at the shop went badly, you say? Sit. Your Hrithik kaka will tell you about my first month running the dhaba on the Pune highway. On the last day of that month, a customer shouted that the dal was cold and walked out without paying. I sat on the step that night, ready to close the whole thing.

Then I remembered what my father did with his accounts. Two columns. So I took the order book and wrote: went well, did not. Went well: the truck drivers came back three nights in a row. The new tandoor worked. The last week was our busiest. Did not: the dal went cold on the busy night.

Three against one. The one was real. The next week I bought a second burner so the dal stayed hot. But I didn't close. The two columns decided that, not the shouting man.

qa.q: What was young Hrithik feeling on the step that night?
qa.a: Young Hrithik felt discouraged and hurt, ready to close the dhaba after one customer's shouting.

qa.q: What turning point in the story let Hrithik decide wisely?
qa.a: Writing two columns, three things that went well and one that didn't, which led him to fix the dal with a second burner instead of closing.

qa.q: How might the truck drivers see the dhaba?
qa.a: They clearly liked it, coming back three nights in a row.

grounding: An uncle recalls listing three things that went well beside one that didn't before deciding whether to close his first dhaba.

Dilnaz's first workshop for the women's self-help group in Leh went through a power cut, a late bus that brought half the participants forty minutes late, and a projector that never worked. At the end, one woman said sharply, "Too much talking, not enough practice."

That evening Dilnaz wanted to cancel the next session. Pema, her co-facilitator, handed her a notebook. "Before you decide, write three things that worked."

Dilnaz sighed. Then she wrote: Everyone stayed till the end, despite the cold. Two women asked for the recipe cards to take home. The group laughed together during introductions.

Under it, she wrote the criticism: Too much talking, not enough practice. It was real, and fair.

"So?" Pema asked.

"So next time, half the session is practice," Dilnaz said. "And we don't cancel."

qa.q: How late did half the participants arrive?
qa.a: Half the participants arrived forty minutes late.

qa.q: How did Dilnaz feel that evening before writing the list?
qa.a: Dilnaz felt discouraged and wanted to cancel the next session because of one sharp criticism.

qa.q: Why did listing three good things first help Dilnaz decide?
qa.a: It balanced her attention, so she could accept the fair criticism and change the plan without abandoning the workshop.

qa.q: How might the two women who asked for recipe cards have felt?
qa.a: They were probably pleased and interested, wanting to take something home from the session.

grounding: Shows a young facilitator who lists three things that went well beside one fair criticism before deciding what to do.

After her first public talk at the Chennai city library, on the history of the old Madras trams, Alka stood by the tea urn replaying one sentence. An old gentleman had said, "You spoke too fast, young lady. Half of us couldn't follow."

On the auto ride home, her friend Elizabeth watched her stare out of the window. "You're doing the thing," Elizabeth said. "Where one comment becomes the whole evening."

Alka laughed weakly. "Maybe."
"Three good things. Go."
Alka thought. "The hall was full. The woman whose grandfather drove a tram came up and cried. And the librarian asked me to do another one in March."
"And the one that didn't?"
"I spoke too fast." She nodded. "That's fair. I'll mark pauses in my notes next time."
"Three and one," Elizabeth said. "Now you can decide."

qa.q: What was Alka's talk about?
qa.a: The talk was about the history of the old Madras trams.

qa.q: What was Alka feeling by the tea urn?
qa.a: Alka felt stung and deflated, replaying the one comment about speaking too fast.

qa.q: What did listing three good things let Alka do?
qa.a: It balanced her view so she could accept the fair criticism, plan pauses in her notes, and still see the talk as a success.

qa.q: How might the woman whose grandfather drove a tram have experienced the talk?
qa.a: She was deeply moved, enough to come up and cry, finding a personal connection in Alka's talk.

grounding: Shows a young woman who, after her first talk, lists three things that went well beside the one fair criticism.

After my first big client workshop, one participant wrote on the feedback card: "Too much theory, not enough practice." I remember my face going hot as I read it on the train home. My old habit would have been to replay that card all weekend.
Instead I did what Zainab, my mentor, taught me. On a page of my notebook, I drew two columns. On the left, three things that worked: the group exercise got people laughing and talking; the client asked me to run a second session; two participants stayed back to ask questions. On the right, the one that didn't: too much theory.
Seeing them side by side, I didn't pretend the card was wrong. It was fair. So I decided to cut two theory slides and add one more exercise.
But I also didn't decide I was bad at workshops. Three and one.
— Naveen

qa.q: What did the participant write on the feedback card?
qa.a: "Too much theory, not enough practice."

qa.q: How did Naveen feel reading the card on the train?
qa.a: Naveen felt embarrassed and stung, face going hot, and was tempted to replay the card all weekend.

qa.q: What did the two columns help Naveen decide?
qa.a: To cut two theory slides and add an exercise, taking the criticism seriously without deciding Naveen was bad at workshops.

qa.q: What might Zainab feel on seeing Naveen's notebook page?
qa.a: Zainab would probably feel glad and proud that the method helped Naveen stay balanced.

Mentor's note, new teachers' programme, by Vandana
Observed Arnab's Class 7 lesson today and met him after. He opened with, "The back row wasn't paying attention. The lesson was a mess." I asked him to try an exercise we'd practised: three things that worked, then the one that didn't, before deciding what to change.
He wrote: 1. The opening question got hands up across the room. 2. His explanation of fractions using rotis was clear, and two children said "oh!" at the same moment. 3. He stayed calm when the projector failed.
Then: The back row drifted after twenty minutes.
He looked at the list for a while. "It wasn't a mess," he said. "The back row is a real problem, though." I agreed with both.
What I did next: we planned a short pair activity at the twenty-minute mark, and I'll observe again next Tuesday.

qa.q: How did Arnab feel right after the lesson, and how did the list change that?

qa.q: What did Vandana and Arnab plan, and why does it fit the list?
